conflicts/second-third-crusades/religion: Both crusades were proclaimed by popes in direct response to Muslim victories (the fall of Edessa in 1144 and the loss of Jerusalem in 1187), were preached as penitential pilgrimages with indulgences, and drew kings into armed pilgrimage on an unprecedented scale. Political rivalries nonetheless shaped them deeply: the choice to attack Damascus in 1148, the Anglo-French quarrels of 1190–1192 and the succession disputes in the Kingdom of Jerusalem. On the Muslim side Zengi, Nur ad-Din and Saladin deliberately cultivated the ideology of jihad to unite Syria and Egypt, though historians such as Lyons and Jackson stress how much Saladin's career also served dynastic ambition.

conflicts/second-third-crusades/sides/1/: Zengid and Ayyubid Syria and Egypt
conflicts/second-third-crusades/sides/4/: Jewish communities of the Rhineland and England (victims)
conflicts/second-third-crusades/summary: The fall of Edessa to Zengi in 1144 prompted Eugenius III and Bernard of Clairvaux to launch the Second Crusade (1145–1149), led by the kings of France and Germany; it ended in defeat in Anatolia and a failed four-day siege of Damascus. Four decades later Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at Hattin and took Jerusalem (1187). The Third Crusade (1189–1192) under Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II and Richard I recaptured Acre and the coast but not Jerusalem, ending in a negotiated truce that allowed Christian pilgrims access to the holy places.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/story:
On 24 December 1144 Imad al-Din Zengi, atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo, captured Edessa, capital of the first crusader state. Pope Eugenius III, a Cistercian, issued the bull Quantum praedecessores on 1 December 1145, the first crusade bull to set out formally the privileges of crusaders. Bernard of Clairvaux, the most influential churchman of the age, preached at Vézelay on 31 March 1146 before Louis VII of France and later persuaded the reluctant Conrad III of Germany to take the cross at Speyer at Christmas 1146. Bernard's preaching letters promised a 'year of jubilee' and remission of sins. The crusade was extended to Iberia, where it helped the capture of Lisbon in 1147, and to the pagan Wends east of the Elbe.

As in 1096, popular preaching turned against Jews. A Cistercian monk named Radulf preached in the Rhineland that Jews should be killed, and attacks followed at Cologne, Mainz, Würzburg and elsewhere. Bernard travelled to the Rhineland, silenced Radulf and wrote that the Jews were not to be persecuted, killed or put to flight, since they were living reminders of Christ's passion and destined for conversion; Jewish chroniclers such as Ephraim of Bonn credited him with saving many lives.

The kings' armies travelled overland through Hungary to Constantinople, where Manuel I Komnenos, then at war with Roger II of Sicily and distrustful after the First Crusade, hurried them across the Bosporus. Conrad's army was routed by the Seljuks near Dorylaeum in October 1147; Louis' army was mauled at Mount Cadmus in January 1148, and many of his poorer followers were abandoned at Attalia. The surviving leaders met at Acre in June 1148 and decided to attack Damascus, a Muslim city that had often been allied with Jerusalem against Zengi. The siege lasted only from 24 to 28 July before the army withdrew amid recriminations. The failure was a shock to the West; Bernard, in his treatise On Consideration, defended the crusade by blaming the sins of the crusaders and comparing the outcome to Israel's failures in the wilderness.

In the following decades Zengi's son Nur ad-Din united Muslim Syria, took Damascus in 1154 and promoted jihad through mosques, madrasas and propaganda centred on Jerusalem. His Kurdish officer Saladin became master of Egypt in 1169, abolished the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and after Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 gradually added Damascus, Aleppo (1183) and Mosul's submission (1186). The Kingdom of Jerusalem, weakened by the leprosy of Baldwin IV and factional disputes, was provoked by Reynald of Châtillon's raids on caravans and on the Red Sea. On 4 July 1187 Saladin destroyed the kingdom's field army at the Horns of Hattin, capturing King Guy of Lusignan and the relic of the True Cross. He personally killed Reynald and had about two hundred captured Templars and Hospitallers executed. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187; Saladin allowed inhabitants to ransom themselves, with no general massacre, although thousands who could not pay were enslaved. Only Tyre, defended by Conrad of Montferrat, and a few castles held out.

Pope Gregory VIII issued the bull Audita tremendi in October 1187, interpreting the disaster as punishment for sin. Henry II of England and Philip II of France imposed the 'Saladin tithe', the first general European tax. Frederick I Barbarossa left Regensburg in May 1189 with a large, disciplined army, forced passage through Byzantine territory and defeated the Seljuks at Iconium (Konya), but drowned in the river Saleph in Cilicia on 10 June 1190, after which most of his army dispersed. In England Richard I's coronation in September 1189 was followed by anti-Jewish riots in London and elsewhere, and in March 1190 the Jews of York, besieged in the royal castle, mostly killed themselves or were murdered after surrender.

Meanwhile Guy of Lusignan, released by Saladin, began a siege of Acre in August 1189, and was himself besieged by Saladin's army in a war of attrition lasting two years. Philip II arrived in April 1191 and Richard in June, having conquered Cyprus from Isaac Komnenos on the way. Acre surrendered on 12 July 1191. When the ransom terms were delayed Richard had about 2,600–3,000 Muslim prisoners killed in sight of Saladin's camp on 20 August. Philip returned to France. Richard defeated Saladin at Arsuf on 7 September 1191, rebuilt Jaffa and twice advanced within sight of Jerusalem but judged that he could not hold it. After further fighting at Jaffa in 1192, Richard and Saladin agreed the Treaty of Jaffa on 2 September 1192: a three-year truce leaving the coast from Tyre to Jaffa to the Latins and Jerusalem to Saladin, with Christian pilgrims allowed to visit the Holy Sepulchre. Richard was captured on his way home and held for ransom by Duke Leopold of Austria and Emperor Henry VI; Saladin died in Damascus in March 1193.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/nameOfGo: Eugenius III's Quantum praedecessores and Gregory VIII's Audita tremendi offered remission of sins and placed crusaders' families and property under church protection. Bernard of Clairvaux preached the crusade as God's gift of an opportunity for salvation to sinners, a 'time of acceptance'. Crusaders took vows and the cross, the True Cross was carried into battle at Hattin, and the loss of Jerusalem was interpreted as divine punishment for sin. Richard I invoked the Holy Sepulchre and crusade privileges, and the Saladin tithe was levied as a holy obligation. On the Muslim side Nur ad-Din and Saladin promoted jihad to recover al-Quds (Jerusalem), the third holiest site of Islam, and Saladin's secretaries Imad al-Din and al-Qadi al-Fadil framed his wars as holy war; Saladin restored the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa as Islamic shrines in 1187.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/religiou: The fall of Edessa in 1144 and of Jerusalem in 1187 were perceived in the West as catastrophes for Christendom requiring a penitential response.
Papal crusade bulls and the preaching of Bernard of Clairvaux and others offered spiritual rewards for taking the cross.
Devotion to Jerusalem and the Holy Sepulchre and the duty to defend the Christian settlers in the East.
The Muslim jihad revival under Zengi, Nur ad-Din and Saladin, centred on the recovery of Jerusalem.
Anti-Jewish preaching by figures such as Radulf, which turned crusading fervour against European Jews.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/otherCau: The political and military weakness of the crusader states, divided by factions and dependent on Western help.
The unification of Syria and Egypt under Nur ad-Din and Saladin, which shifted the regional balance of power.
Royal ambitions and rivalries, notably between the Capetian and Angevin kings, and the prestige of crusading kingship.
The commercial interests of Italian maritime cities in the Levantine ports.
Byzantine–Latin tensions and Byzantine diplomacy with the Seljuks and Saladin.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/triggers: Zengi's capture of Edessa on 24 December 1144.
Reynald of Châtillon's attacks on Muslim caravans in breach of truces, which provoked Saladin's invasion of 1187.
The defeat at Hattin on 4 July 1187 and the surrender of Jerusalem on 2 October 1187.

conflicts/second-third-crusades/casualti: No reliable overall figure exists. Chroniclers' numbers for the armies of 1147–1148 and 1189–1192 are greatly exaggerated; losses from disease and famine, especially at the two-year siege of Acre, were very heavy on both sides. Specific events are better attested: about 200 Templars and Hospitallers executed after Hattin, about 2,600–3,000 Muslim prisoners killed at Acre in 1191, and roughly 150 Jews dead at York in 1190, though even these are approximate.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/effects/: The Second Crusade's failure discredited crusading for a generation and strengthened Nur ad-Din's position.
Saladin's unification of Egypt and Syria and his victory at Hattin ended the first Kingdom of Jerusalem's control of the interior.
The Third Crusade restored a coastal 'second kingdom' of Jerusalem with Acre as capital, which survived for a century.
Cyprus became a Latin kingdom under the Lusignans, lasting until 1489.
The Saladin tithe set a precedent for general taxation for crusades and later for royal taxation.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/effectsO: Crusading was extended formally to Iberia and the Baltic in 1147, diversifying its targets.
Papal theology of crusade as penance was reinforced by explaining defeats as punishment for sin.
Bernard's intervention restated the church's doctrine that Jews must not be killed, but anti-Jewish violence became a recurring accompaniment of crusade preaching, notably in England in 1189–1190.
The military orders gained wealth, castles and influence in the East and in Europe.
Muslim control of Jerusalem from 1187 restricted Latin worship there, while Saladin allowed Eastern Christian clergy to remain at the Holy Sepulchre.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/legacy: Richard and Saladin became legendary figures of chivalry in both European and Middle Eastern memory, and Saladin's recapture of Jerusalem has been invoked by many modern Arab leaders. The York massacre is commemorated today at Clifford's Tower. The repeated failures of large royal expeditions led to new approaches, including the Fourth Crusade's plan to attack Egypt, which ended at Constantinople instead.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/dissente: While preaching the crusade, Bernard opposed the monk Radulf, writing to the Rhineland clergy that Jews must not be persecuted, killed or driven out, since 'the Jews are for us the living words of Scripture'.

An anonymous chronicler at Würzburg (Annales Herbipolenses) wrote that the Second Crusade was promoted by 'pseudo-prophets, sons of Belial' and that its failure showed God had not approved it, one of the sharpest contemporary criticisms of crusading.

The English cleric, in De re militari et triplici via peregrinationis Ierosolimitane (c. 1187–1188), questioned whether the recovery of Jerusalem justified killing Muslims, criticised the Saladin tithe and argued that Muslims should be won by preaching rather than the sword.
The Cistercian abbot criticised the new military orders as a 'new monstrosity', questioning a form of religious life devoted to killing unbelievers in the name of Christ.
conflicts/second-third-crusades/theatres: Defeat of Conrad III near Dorylaeum
Massacre of the Jews of York (Clifford's Tower)
Siege of Acre and killing of prisoners
conflicts/second-third-crusades/campaign: Louis VII's march to the East, 1147–1148
Louis VII, Eleanor of Aquitaine and the French army

The French marched through Germany and Hungary to Constantinople, followed the Anatolian coast to Ephesus, were mauled at Mount Cadmus beyond Laodicea, sailed from Attalia to Antioch, and joined the council at Acre that chose to besiege Damascus.
Emperor Frederick I and the German army

Barbarossa's army crossed Hungary and the Balkans, occupied Philippopolis and Adrianople in a dispute with Byzantium, crossed the Hellespont at Gallipoli, stormed Iconium and reached Cilicia, where the emperor drowned.
Richard I and the Anglo-Norman fleet and army

Richard set out with Philip II from Vézelay, sailed from Marseille, wintered at Messina, conquered Cyprus, joined the siege of Acre, marched down the coast to victory at Arsuf, and concluded the war at Jaffa.
